title: Working on a table top simulator
author: That1guy4226
selftext:
So I wanted to roll a lot of dice at once and see them actually roll so I started making a rolling app. then it kept evolving to what is becoming a table top simulation style VTT. I have also added a bunch of maps and models that can be placed and moved around. 

Im sorry if the recording looks like crap, I only have 8 gigs of ram so recording while using it was tricky but it can roll up to 10,000 dice at once currently. Though I lose framerates around 1200 or so.

I could really use some help or advice and getting some feedback on it. it is available to try but it is still an early work in progress.

comments.author: ledniv
comments.body:
The 10,000-dice test is a great place to start profiling this. If every die is a GameObject with a Rigidbody + collider, I’d expect Unity Physics to become the bottleneck long before memory itself does.

One approach would be to separate the **dice state from the dice GameObjects**. Keep position, velocity, rotation, result, etc. as data, process as much as possible in batches, and let the GameObjects just visualize that state. For very large rolls, you could even switch from full physics to a cheaper simulated/fake roll once the count passes some threshold — the player probably doesn’t need 10,000 individually accurate PhysX simulations to believe they rolled.

The important thing is to profile CPU, physics, and rendering separately before optimizing. AI can generate a lot of working code very quickly, but it will happily give every die its own scripts/Update/physics state unless you give it architectural rules.

Small plug: this kind of data-first optimization is what I cover in *High Performance Unity Game Development with Data-Oriented Design*:

[https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development](https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development)
